section.title: A Cry for Mercy in Distress
section.sectionRationale: The first of the traditional penitential psalms, a raw lament from physical and emotional agony that turns, without any narrated resolution, into sudden confidence that the LORD has heard.
section.thesis: David, weak in body and flooded with weeping, asks God not to rebuke him in anger but to heal and deliver him for the sake of His loving devotion, and even before his circumstances change, declares that the LORD has heard his cry for mercy.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the opening cry from bodily and emotional agony (vv1-3), the plea for deliverance grounded in God's loving devotion (vv4-7), and the sudden turn to confidence that the LORD has heard, putting his enemies to shame (vv8-10).

units.label: A cry from agony
units.note: how long, O LORD, how long

verses.text: O LORD, do not rebuke me in Your anger or discipline me in Your wrath.
Be merciful to me, O LORD, for I am frail; heal me, O LORD, for my bones are in agony.
My soul is deeply distressed. How long, O LORD, how long?

units.label: Deliver me for Your loving devotion
units.note: no mention of You in death

verses.text: Turn, O LORD, and deliver my soul; save me because of Your {{chesed|loving devotion}}.
For there is no mention of You in death; who can praise You from Sheol?
I am weary from groaning; all night I flood my bed with weeping and drench my couch with tears.
My eyes fail from grief; they grow dim because of all my foes.

units.label: The LORD has heard
units.note: depart, all you workers of iniquity

verses.text: Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity, for the LORD has heard my weeping.
The LORD has heard my cry for mercy; the LORD accepts my prayer.
All my enemies will be ashamed and dismayed; they will turn back in sudden disgrace.

chesed.gloss: Steadfast love, loyal covenant devotion. David appeals to this, not his own innocence, as the reason God should save him, showing that even in deep affliction the ground of hope is God's committed character rather than the sufferer's merit.

basic.context: Psalm 6 is the first of the seven traditional penitential psalms, a raw cry from physical weakness and overwhelming grief. David asks God not to discipline him in anger but to heal him because of His loving devotion, and, remarkably, without any narrated change in circumstances, declares partway through that the LORD has heard his weeping.
basic.hermeneutics: This is honest lament prayer, not stoic resignation; the psalm gives full voice to physical agony, sleepless weeping, and fear of death, and models how genuine faith can hold together unresolved suffering with sudden, confident assurance that God has heard, even before anything visibly changes.
basic.originalLanguages: David appeals to God's chesed, His steadfast covenant love, as the reason to be saved, not his own innocence. His argument in verse 5, that the dead do not praise God from Sheol, is not a doctrine of the afterlife but an urgent appeal, as if to say, save me now, so that I may go on praising You.
basic.typology: David's cry from bodily agony and near despair, met by sudden assurance of being heard, anticipates Christ's own cries of anguish, met by the Father, and every believer's confidence that prayers offered in weakness are truly heard even before deliverance is seen.
basic.christ: Jesus, in Gethsemane, cried out in similarly deep anguish, His soul overwhelmed to the point of death, Matthew 26:38, and was heard by His Father, Hebrews 5:7, modeling exactly the pattern David lives out here: honest agony met by confident trust that God hears.
basic.god: God disciplines out of love, not mere anger, yet David can appeal past that discipline to God's own loving devotion, trusting that the same God who allows affliction is the one who will hear, heal, and turn his enemies back in shame.
basic.crossReferences: Hebrews 5:7 describes Christ's own loud cries and tears heard by the Father. Matthew 7:23 echoes the phrase 'depart from Me' in reverse, used later of Christ Himself rejecting workers of iniquity. Psalm 30:5 promises that weeping may last the night but joy comes in the morning.
basic.oneStory: Psalm 6 gives voice to the believer's darkest nights, bodily agony, sleepless grief, and fear of death, and teaches that even there, before anything changes, the LORD hears. Christ entered exactly this kind of anguish for us, and was heard, so that every cry of ours joined to His is certain to be heard as well.

context.literary:
The psalm is shaped like a descent followed by a sudden lift. Verses 1 to 3 begin with the pleading, verses 4 to 7 give the reasons, and verses 8 to 10 turn to an announcement. There is no gradual climb out of the pit. The mood flips between one verse and the next, from a person who is soaking his bed with tears to one who tells his enemies to leave.

One Hebrew verb holds the whole thing together. It means to be shaken or terrified, and it lands on three different subjects. In verse 2 David's bones are shaken, in verse 3 his soul is shaken, and in verse 10 his enemies are shaken. The BSB renders it 'agony,' 'deeply distressed,' and 'dismayed,' so the echo is hidden in English. The fear that shakes the body and the soul of the sufferer is handed over at the end to those who caused it.

A second thread is the word for turning. In verse 4 David begs the LORD to 'turn,' and in verse 10 the enemies 'turn back' in disgrace. The prayer that God will turn toward him is answered by a turn that sends the enemy away. The movements of the psalm are two-way traffic: God turns toward the sufferer, and the foes are turned around.

The body dominates: bones, soul, eyes, bed, couch. The name of the LORD is repeated again and again through the first four verses as a cry, and in verses 8 and 9 it appears as the subject of the verb 'has heard.' The frantic prayer of the opening does not fade; it is met, and the LORD who was addressed becomes the LORD who acts.

The question 'How long, O LORD, how long?' is left unfinished in verse 3, a sentence with no ending. It reads like a person whose speech has run out, and the psalm shows that the unfinished sentence is heard just the same.
context.historical:
The heading directs the psalm to the choirmaster, with stringed instruments, 'according to Sheminith,' and gives it to David. The BSB notes that Sheminith is probably a musical term, found also in 1 Chronicles 15:21 and Psalm 12. Its exact meaning is not known, and the safest thing to say is that the psalm was meant to be sung in worship and not only whispered in private.

Nothing in the psalm names the illness or the enemy. That silence is part of its use. A person in ancient Israel did not have a clean line between sickness, enemies and God's displeasure. Pain of the body could be read as a sign that God was angry, and enemies would gloat over a sick man, as the psalm's language suggests. Elsewhere David's sickness is described in similar terms, Psalm 38:1-4, and both psalms open with almost the same words about anger and wrath, Psalm 6:1 and Psalm 38:1.

For the first hearers, the prospect of death was frightening in a particular way. Sheol was not a place of punishment for the wicked so much as the place where life's praise fell silent. Israel spoke of the dead as those who no longer join in the songs of the temple, Psalm 115:17. A worshipper in the sanctuary depended on being alive to give thanks, and it is that logic that drives verse 5.

The sound of weeping through the night has a real setting in the poor man's house. A bed drenched with tears is not a figure of speech for someone who has not slept. The psalm was written for people who knew that kind of night and needed words to bring to God when their own failed. Its use in worship meant that a congregation could sing beside the sick and the slandered.
context.canonical:
From the early church onward, Psalm 6 has been counted first among the seven penitential psalms, with Psalms 32, 38, 51, 102, 130 and 143. The label fits some of these better than others, because Psalm 6 never names a sin. What it shares with them is the plea to be treated with mercy and not with the full weight of wrath. Its first verse is nearly the same as Psalm 38:1, and Psalm 38 makes the link with sin plain: 'there is no rest in my bones because of my sin,' Psalm 38:3.

The claim that the dead cannot praise God returns in other prayers. Psalm 30:9 asks 'Will the dust praise You?' and Psalm 88:10-12 lists the questions one by one. Hezekiah reasons the same way when he faces death, 'the living, only the living, can thank You, as I do today,' Isaiah 38:19. The psalm's argument is not a lecture on the afterlife but a shared way of pleading for life.

Psalm 6 is also taken up by Jesus. In Matthew 7:23 He says to those who claim Him without knowing Him, 'depart from Me, you workers of lawlessness,' echoing verse 8 nearly word for word. Luke has the same warning, 'Depart from me, all you evildoers,' Luke 13:27. The text David sang against his persecutors becomes the sentence of the Judge on those who never knew Him.

The New Testament also shows how the psalm's agony is taken into the life of Jesus. John 12:27 has Him say, 'Now My soul is troubled,' and Matthew 26:38 has Him say, 'My soul is consumed with sorrow to the point of death.' The last cries of the sufferer become the prayer of the Son.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
David gave the worshipper words for the night when praise is hard. He wanted Israel to see that a person in agony is not to keep quiet until he feels better. The right thing is to bring the whole weight of distress into the presence of the LORD, including the request that God not be angry, the fear of death, and the complaint of exhaustion.

He also meant to show what a prayer of faith looks like at its lowest point. There is no boast of innocence, no bargain and no promise to do better. The one argument David makes is that God is loving and that the dead cannot praise Him. He appeals to who God is and to the shared purpose of God and His people, which is that the LORD be praised by the living.

The final movement is where the psalm teaches most. David does not wait for the pain to end before he announces that the LORD has heard. He tells his enemies to leave because the LORD has heard his weeping, and his certainty comes from the character of the One who listens and not from an improvement in his health. Israel was meant to learn that a prayer, once offered, is already in the ear of God, and that a believer may speak as though the answer has begun.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes one person's suffering: the bed soaked with tears, the failing eyes and the enemies who gather. It does not say that every illness is a sign of God's anger, and it does not teach that grief is a sin. Job's friends made the mistake of treating suffering as proof of guilt, and Scripture rejects it. Verse 1 asks not to be disciplined in wrath; it does not claim that this trouble is a punishment.

What it prescribes by example is a manner of praying. Tell God plainly how your body and soul feel. Ask for mercy on the ground of His loving devotion and not your merit. Let the fear of death move you to plead for life so that you may go on praising Him. Then say out loud, before anything has changed, that the LORD has heard.

A note of care is needed for verse 8. David's word to the wicked is a declaration of confidence and not permission to drive people away. Jesus makes the same words a verdict at the last judgment, Matthew 7:23, which is a matter for Him and not for us. In our own day the right use of verses 8 to 10 is to place hostile people in God's hands and to trust that shame and turning are His to give.

debates.question: Is Psalm 6 really a penitential psalm?

views.label: Yes, it is a prayer of a sinner under discipline
views.case: The psalm begins by asking not to be rebuked in anger, and to be healed and saved because of God's loving devotion. The church's early listing of it among the penitential psalms reflects the reading that suffering here is tied to God's displeasure, as in Psalm 38:1-4.

views.label: No, it is a lament of the afflicted that never confesses a sin
views.case: David does not name a sin or ask to be forgiven. The enemies of verses 7 to 10 seem to be the source of his trouble, and Job shows that suffering does not always come from guilt. He asks to be spared anger, which could mean that he is not claiming to deserve it.

views.label: It is both, and the psalm leaves the cause open on purpose
views.case: Because the psalm names neither a sin nor a cause, any sufferer can pray it, whether the trouble comes from his own folly, from enemies or from illness. The openness is the design.

debates.bearing: The prayer works in every case. If sin is in view, the appeal to loving devotion is where forgiveness is found, Psalm 130:3-4. If it is not, the psalm still shows that a righteous person can plead with God for mercy without needing to prove his innocence.

debates.question: What explains the sudden change at verse 8?

views.label: An oracle of salvation was given between verses 7 and 8
views.case: Some hold that a priest or prophet spoke a word of assurance in the sanctuary, so that the change of mood answers a reply from God. The psalm would then record the moment the LORD spoke.

views.label: Faith itself arrives at certainty through prayer
views.case: Others point out that the psalm mentions no reply and that the change comes through the act of praying. The sufferer lays out his case and comes to see, in the presence of God, that it has been heard, as in Psalm 28:6, 'Blessed be the LORD, for He has heard my cry for mercy.'

views.label: The psalm was completed after the rescue
views.case: A third view is that the last verses were written or sung after the deliverance and joined to the earlier lament. The verbs 'has heard' then look back on what God has done.

debates.bearing: The text does not settle the origin of the turn, and its meaning does not depend on it. In every case the psalm teaches that the certainty of being heard can arrive before the relief and that both belong to the LORD.

debates.question: Does verse 5 teach that there is no conscious life or praise after death?

views.label: It reflects the limited light of the Old Testament
views.case: The silence of the dead is affirmed elsewhere, Psalm 115:17, and the full hope of resurrection awaits later revelation, when Christ 'abolished death and illuminated the way to life and immortality,' 2 Timothy 1:10.

views.label: It is a plea and not a doctrine
views.case: David argues from the worshipper's point of view, that living praise is what he is asking to keep. The verse does not lay out a theology of the dead but appeals to God's own interest in being praised.

debates.bearing: Read either way, the verse should not be used to deny resurrection. It gives the fear of death a voice, and the gospel answers that fear, 1 Corinthians 15:54-55.

study.originalLanguages:
The verb behind the triple echo of verses 2, 3 and 10 is bahal, to be shaken or dismayed. It suggests sudden terror, a trembling that runs through a person. Because it lands on David's bones, his soul and finally his enemies, the psalm reads as a reversal. What has been done to him is finally done to them.

In verse 1 the two verbs for God's response are yakhach and yasar. The first is to rebuke or reprove, as in a legal setting, and the second is to discipline, teach or correct. They belong to the language of a father's training in Proverbs 3:11-12, where the LORD disciplines the one He loves. David does not ask to escape all correction. He asks that it not be delivered in anger and wrath, which is a different request.

Verse 2 says he is 'frail.' The Hebrew word suggests withering, a plant left without water. It sits beside 'heal me,' the Hebrew rapha, the same verb the LORD uses of Himself in Exodus 15:26. The bones of the psalm belong to the same picture: a body drying up and a God who can restore it. In verse 4 he asks God to 'turn,' from the root that also gives the word for repentance, and to 'deliver my soul,' using nefesh, the whole living self, not a detached part. Verse 3 says that 'my soul' is shaken, and verse 4 asks that this same soul be rescued.

The word translated 'Sheol' in verse 5 is a name for the place of the dead. It is paired here with zeker, 'mention' or remembrance, and this is the word that is normally used of remembering God's name and deeds in worship. In the sanctuary a person remembered the LORD out loud. In Sheol no one does.

The verbs for weeping in verse 6 pile up in an exaggeration on purpose: he 'floods' his bed and 'drenches' his couch. The words picture not a gentle tear but a bed swimming in water. In verse 8 the workers of iniquity, po'ale aven, are the same class of people who appear in Psalm 5:5, so the psalms sit side by side with the same enemy.

The last words of the psalm have a sound to them. 'Sudden' in verse 10 is rega, the word for an instant, a blink. The enemies who caused such long weeping are undone in a moment, which fits a psalm in which the night has been long and the reversal is swift.

typology.type: The sufferer whose soul is shaken, Psalm 6:2-3
typology.fulfillment: David's bones and soul are shaken with dread. The pattern reaches Jesus, who says 'Now My soul is troubled,' John 12:27, and, in Gethsemane, 'My soul is consumed with sorrow to the point of death,' Matthew 26:38. The correspondence is deeper in Christ, because His anguish was not for His own sins but for the cup He was to drink for others. The type falls short because David's suffering could not save anyone else, while the agony of Jesus is the road to the salvation of the many, Hebrews 2:10.

typology.type: The prayer heard without the removal of the cup, Psalm 6:9
typology.fulfillment: David is sure that the LORD has heard and accepts his prayer even before the trouble ends. Hebrews describes the Son who 'offered up prayers and petitions with loud cries and tears to the One who could save Him from death, and He was heard because of His reverence,' Hebrews 5:7. He was heard, and He was raised. The correspondence is that prayer in weakness is genuinely heard. The escalation is that the Son is heard by being brought through death and not around it, and the type falls short in that David's deliverance was temporary, while Christ's is an eternal resurrection.

typology.type: Sheol and the silence of the dead, Psalm 6:5
typology.fulfillment: The fear that the grave ends all praise is answered in Christ, who 'has abolished death and illuminated the way to life and immortality through the gospel,' 2 Timothy 1:10. Paul quotes 'Death has been swallowed up in victory' in 1 Corinthians 15:54. What David feared as the end of worship becomes, for those in Christ, a passage to the presence of God. The type falls short only in being a fear without an answer, and the answer is not fully seen until the day when death itself is no more, Revelation 21:4.

study.christ:
The psalm points to Christ by the pattern of the suffering servant who prays. John records the moment when Jesus said, 'Now My soul is troubled, and what shall I say? "Father, save Me from this hour"? No, it is for this purpose that I have come to this hour,' John 12:27. The words 'my soul is troubled' recall Psalm 6:3, where the soul is shaken, and the Greek Old Testament uses a verb from the same family. The Lord does not treat David's psalm as a curiosity; He makes it His own.

It points to Christ in Gethsemane. Matthew says He 'began to be sorrowful and deeply distressed,' Matthew 26:37, and told His disciples His soul was consumed with sorrow to the point of death, verse 38. Luke adds that in His anguish He prayed more earnestly, Luke 22:44. Hebrews 5:7 sums up such scenes: loud cries and tears to the One who could save Him from death, and He was heard. Psalm 6 is where David lays out the language of that prayer, and the Gospels show that the Son prayed it in fact.

The psalm also points to Christ as the sympathetic priest. Hebrews 4:15 says we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses. The Word who wept at the grave of Lazarus, John 11:35, understands the person whose bed is wet with tears. The believer who prays Psalm 6 is not speaking to a distant God, but to one who has been in the room of weeping and has come out of it.

It points to Christ by the answer to verse 5. The fear that no praise rises from Sheol is met in the resurrection. Christ has 'abolished death,' 2 Timothy 1:10, and the perishable will be clothed with the imperishable, 1 Corinthians 15:54. Because He was raised, the dead in Christ will praise, and the silence of Sheol is broken.

Finally, the discipline in verse 1 has a shadow in the cross. Hebrews 12:5-6 says the Lord disciplines the one He loves, and Romans 8:1 says there is now no condemnation for those in Christ Jesus. David asks not to be rebuked in wrath; the gospel says that the wrath fell on Christ so that those in Him receive fatherly discipline and never condemnation.

We should be careful not to make Christ the speaker of every clause. The pleas about frailty and the plea for pardon of any sin are David's, and Jesus, being sinless, does not pray for forgiveness of His own. But the dread, the tears and the assurance of being heard are His, and every believer's, in Him.
study.god:
Psalm 6 shows a God who can be spoken to about His own anger. That is a remarkable thing. David does not pretend the LORD is never angry; he asks that anger not be the manner of His correction. The prayer assumes that the LORD is holy enough to be angry, and loving enough to be asked to hold back. It sets the fear of God and the hope of mercy beside each other.

He is a God of chesed. The single ground David offers for rescue is 'Your loving devotion,' verse 4. God's faithfulness to His covenant is the argument. It is sometimes called a strange argument to use with a God who could simply choose otherwise, but Scripture treats it as the only one that is sure, because God has bound Himself by promise. Psalm 103:8-10 says He is slow to anger and abounding in loving devotion, and that He has not dealt with us according to our sins.

He is the God who hears. The threefold repetition in verses 8 and 9, 'the LORD has heard my weeping,' 'the LORD has heard my cry for mercy,' 'the LORD accepts my prayer,' makes hearing a settled fact. Tears are not lost. Psalm 22:24 says He 'has not despised or detested the torment of the afflicted,' and the wise reader sees that this belongs to His character and not to David's merit.

He is also the God of life. David bases his plea on the fact that God receives praise from the living, verse 5, and this suggests that God delights in the worship of His people and gives life for that purpose. Psalm 115:17-18 puts the same contrast. The result is that God's glory and the sufferer's survival are not enemies. His purposes are not served by the loss of His people.

He is Judge over those who trouble the faithful. The workers of iniquity are told to depart because the LORD has heard. The enemies are the ones who end up dismayed. This does not require the sufferer to fight, and it does not require him to be well. The LORD deals with them in a moment.

For worship, the psalm teaches that the best response to overwhelming distress is neither silence nor pretence but honest speech aimed at a God who listens. The believer is invited to come with the whole wet pillow and the unfinished question 'how long,' and to leave with the sound of a man who knows he has been heard. That is a kind of praise before praise, and it reflects a God who is patient with the weak and sure in His response.

crossReferences.note: The opening verse is almost identical to Psalm 6:1, and Psalm 38 goes on to tie the bodily suffering to the sufferer's sin and the hand of God upon him. Read beside Psalm 6, it shows how the same plea can be prayed by someone who is guilty as well as by someone who is only afflicted.

Another prayer that argues from the silence of the grave, 'Will the dust praise You?' Here the outcome is recorded: mourning turned to dancing and sackcloth exchanged for joy. It shows what the ending of a Psalm 6 prayer can look like when the answer arrives.

Hezekiah, sick and told to expect death, says that Sheol cannot thank the LORD and 'the living, only the living, can thank You.' It is the same reasoning as Psalm 6:5, and it shows that the argument was a recognised way to plead for life.

A darker sibling of Psalm 6. It asks a run of questions about praise in the grave and ends with no relief. The two psalms together give the church a language for pain that does not hurry to the ending, and both are Scripture.

Jesus tells those who did wonders in His name without knowing Him, 'depart from Me, you workers of lawlessness!' The line echoes Psalm 6:8, and it moves the sentence from David's foes to the final judgment, of which Christ is the Judge.

'Now My soul is troubled.' Jesus voices the shaking of the soul that David describes in Psalm 6:3, and He chooses the hour of the cross instead of asking to be saved from it. The Son takes the sufferer's prayer and completes it in obedience.

Christ's 'loud cries and tears' to the One who could save Him from death, and the note that He was heard. It gives the New Testament ground for the confidence of Psalm 6:8-9, and shows that being heard does not always mean being spared the ordeal.

When we do not know how to pray, the Spirit intercedes with groans too deep for words. Psalm 6:6 is the person who is 'weary from groaning,' and this text tells the believer that even wordless groaning is carried to God.

'The Lord disciplines the one He loves.' David asks to be corrected without wrath, verse 1, and Hebrews teaches that correction from a father is a sign of love. It helps the reader see that the discipline of Psalm 6 is not the same as condemnation.

'If You, O LORD, kept track of iniquities, then who, O Lord, could stand? But with You there is forgiveness.' It answers the question under Psalm 6:1 and the fear behind it. Another of the penitential psalms, it names the forgiveness that Psalm 6 only pleads for.

'Death has been swallowed up in victory.' It is the answer to the silence of Sheol in Psalm 6:5. Because of the resurrection, the fear that death ends praise is overturned, and the dead in Christ will sing.

study.oneStory:
The psalm sits inside the world after Genesis 3, where pain, tears and death are the ordinary lot of human beings. God said to the woman and the man that they would die, and this psalm is what a dying person sounds like when he still believes in the God of life. Its fear of Sheol is the fear that the story of creation, in which humanity was made to praise, is being ended by the curse.

The Old Testament adds voice after voice to this cry. Hezekiah turns his face to the wall, Isaiah 38:2. The sons of Korah write of the dead as those beyond God's wonders, Psalm 88:10-12. The prophets look for a day when death will be undone. None of them has the full answer. They pray in the dark, and the LORD hears, but the great reversal has not yet happened.

The turn comes when the Son of God enters the world of tears. He weeps at a tomb, John 11:35. His soul is troubled, John 12:27. He is sorrowful in a garden, Matthew 26:37. He prays with loud cries, Hebrews 5:7, and He is heard, not by being spared death but by being raised from it. The psalm's fear of the silence of Sheol is answered on the third day. Paul can say that Christ 'abolished death and illuminated the way to life and immortality,' 2 Timothy 1:10.

Until the end, believers still pray this psalm. The Spirit helps them in weakness and intercedes with groans, Romans 8:26. They live in the time when the LORD has heard and the enemy is not yet gone. Discipline continues, but it is the discipline of a Father, and there is no condemnation for those in Christ Jesus, Romans 8:1.

The story ends with the answer to every line of Psalm 6. In the new creation, 'He will wipe away every tear from their eyes,' and there will be 'no more death or mourning or crying or pain,' Revelation 21:4. The bed that was soaked with weeping is replaced by a city in which nobody grieves. The question 'how long' is finally closed. And the dead, whom David feared would fall silent, will join a great company in praise, because the God who hears the weeping of one sufferer has, in Christ, undone the power of death for all who trust Him.

quiz.q: What does David ask God NOT to do in verse 1?

options.text: Rebuke him in anger or discipline him in wrath.
options.note: This is the psalm's opening plea, asking for mercy rather than full wrath.

options.text: Answer his prayer at all.
options.note: David desperately wants to be heard; his plea is against full-force anger, not against being answered.

options.text: Heal his physical body.
options.note: David explicitly asks for healing in verse 2; his plea in verse 1 is against harsh discipline.

options.text: Reveal Himself to David's enemies.
options.note: This is not mentioned in verse 1 at all.

quiz.q: On what basis does David ask to be saved in verse 4?

options.text: For the sake of God's loving devotion, chesed, not his own merit.
options.note: David explicitly grounds his appeal in God's covenant character.

options.text: Because he has never sinned.
options.note: David does not claim sinlessness; he appeals to God's mercy and loving devotion instead.

options.text: Because his enemies are more wicked than he is.
options.note: The appeal is to God's own character, not a comparison of relative wickedness.

options.text: He gives no reason at all.
options.note: Verse 4 explicitly states the reason: God's loving devotion.

quiz.q: How does David describe his nights in verse 6?

options.text: He is weary from groaning, flooding his bed with weeping and drenching his couch with tears all night.
options.note: This vividly pictures the depth of David's ongoing grief and exhaustion.

options.text: He sleeps peacefully despite his troubles.
options.note: This is the opposite of what verse 6 describes; his nights are marked by weeping, not peace.

options.text: He spends his nights planning revenge.
options.note: The verse describes grief and weeping, not scheming or plotting.

options.text: He does not mention his nights at all.
options.note: Verse 6 explicitly describes his nightly weeping in vivid detail.

quiz.q: What sudden shift happens in verses 8-9?

options.text: David declares with confidence that the LORD has heard his weeping and his cry for mercy, even though his circumstances have not visibly changed.
options.note: This is the striking, unresolved turn from lament to confident assurance.

options.text: His enemies suddenly repent and become his friends.
options.note: The shift is in David's own confidence that he has been heard, not a reported change in his enemies' hearts.

options.text: God audibly speaks to David to explain the reason for his suffering.
options.note: No explanation is given; David simply declares his confidence that his prayer has been heard.

options.text: Nothing changes; the psalm ends exactly as it began.
options.note: Verses 8-9 mark a clear and dramatic shift in tone toward confidence.

quiz.q: How does this psalm connect to Christ's experience in Gethsemane?

options.text: Jesus also cried out with loud cries and tears from deep anguish, and was heard by His Father, Hebrews 5:7.
options.note: Hebrews 5:7 directly describes Christ's anguished, heard prayer, paralleling this psalm's pattern.

options.text: Jesus never experienced anguish comparable to this psalm.
options.note: Matthew 26:38 describes Jesus' soul as overwhelmed with sorrow to the point of death, directly comparable anguish.

options.text: The connection is only that both figures prayed at some point.
options.note: The connection is much more specific: both offer anguished cries from deep distress that are heard by God.

options.text: There is no meaningful connection between this psalm and Christ.
options.note: Hebrews 5:7 draws a clear, specific parallel to this kind of anguished, heard prayer.

questions: David brings raw physical and emotional pain honestly to God rather than hiding it. What pain, physical or emotional, are you tempted to keep from God rather than bring openly to Him in prayer?

David appeals to God's loving devotion, not his own innocence, as the reason to be saved. Where are you tempted to believe God's help depends on your own performance rather than His steadfast character?

David's confidence that he has been heard comes before any change in his circumstances. Have you ever experienced this kind of assurance in prayer even while your situation remained the same? What did that feel like?
David flooded his bed with tears night after night; his grief was not quick or tidy. How do you make room for ongoing grief in your own life rather than rushing yourself toward resolution?
Jesus cried out in anguish in Gethsemane and was heard by His Father. How does knowing that Christ Himself prayed through deep anguish change the way you view your own desperate prayers?

translationNotes.note: Rebuke and discipline both describe corrective action, language elsewhere applied to God's fatherly correction of His people, Hebrews 12:5-6, though the psalm does not name a specific sin behind David's suffering.

There is no mention of You in death is a common rhetorical appeal found across the Psalms, urging God to act now so the psalmist can continue praising Him, rather than a settled doctrinal statement about the afterlife.
In sudden disgrace pictures a swift, complete reversal for the enemies, matching the sudden reversal in David's own confidence from verse 7 to verse 8.
